title: Memory and state across turns
story:
The model has no memory. Every request is answered by something that has never seen you before, and every appearance of continuity is a thing your system stored and sent again. Say that plainly before designing anything, because the whole problem changes shape once you accept it: there is no memory feature to configure, there is a retrieval problem you own, with a budget you pay on every turn.

The simplest approach is to send the whole conversation each time, and it works beautifully until it does not. Cost and latency rise with every exchange, because the entire history is reprocessed on each turn. Then the history exceeds what fits, and something truncates it — and what gets dropped is the oldest part, which is where the instructions and the original goal were. The conversation appears to deteriorate. The user says it has got worse, and it has, not because anything degraded but because the beginning fell off the front. This failure is silent, gradual, and almost always diagnosed as the model rather than the plumbing.

Summarising is the usual response, and it has its own trap. Summarise the summary each time and the losses compound: detail disappears, and anything a summary got slightly wrong becomes a fact the next summary inherits and states with more confidence. Summarise from the durable record instead, not from the last summary, so errors cannot accumulate across generations. That one rule removes most of the pain.

Then there is staleness, which is subtler and shows up later. A preference someone expressed once is not permanent. A fact recorded in a conversation was true at that moment, and it will be recited long after it stopped being true unless something makes it expire. Anything you carry forward should have a time attached and a reason to be dropped, and the reason should be written down when you store it rather than invented when it causes an incident.

The most important distinction in this lesson is between conversation state and application state, because mixing them is the failure that costs money. If something must be correct — an order, a balance, an entitlement, a decision with consequences — it lives in your database, with the guarantees your database provides, and the conversation is a view onto it. A transcript is not a record. It cannot be queried, cannot be audited, cannot be transactionally updated, and the model will paraphrase it. The rule is easy to apply and rarely applied: when a turn produces something that matters, write it down as data at that moment, in the shape you would have designed if no model were involved.

That leaves a clean three-part design. What is durable gets written to storage you own as it happens. What is recalled is retrieved per turn based on the current message — not everything so far, but the few things relevant now, which is the same retrieval problem as any other. And what is dropped is most of it, deliberately, with the confidence that anything important was already written down.

One last requirement that is easy to leave for later and then very hard to add. Whatever you carry forward about a person should be visible to them and correctable by them. A system that remembers things about a user, cannot show what it remembers, and cannot be corrected is making claims about them they have no way to dispute. Build the view early. Every system that has one ended up using it for debugging too, because a list of what was carried forward is the first thing you want when the answers start going strange.

problem.name: Reconstructing continuity for a stateless system
problem.shape: Each request is answered with no knowledge of any previous one, and the user expects continuity.
tell: the whole conversation is resent on every turn and the cost grows with its length
a long conversation seems to get worse and nobody can say when it started
summaries are produced from the previous summary
something that has to be correct only exists inside the transcript
the system remembers facts about a user that the user cannot see or change
problem.move: Write anything durable to storage you own at the moment it happens, retrieve per turn only what the current message needs, summarise from the record rather than from the last summary, attach an expiry to what you carry, and give the user a view of it.
problem.invariant: Any continuity the user experiences is something your system stored and resent, so everything about memory is a decision you made rather than a behaviour of the model.
problem.breaks: When the history outgrows the window, truncation silently removes the oldest part, which is usually the instructions and the original goal — so the conversation degrades without any component reporting a fault.

cost.time: resending history reprocesses it on every turn, so latency grows with the length of the conversation
cost.space: the window is the limit, which makes forgetting mandatory and the only question which forgetting you chose
cost.beats: sending everything, which grows without bound and truncates silently, and sending nothing, which is cheap and makes continuity impossible

problem.practice: Take a long conversation with your own system and print exactly what is sent on the twentieth turn. Find the original instructions in it. If they are missing, you have just found the cause of the decline people have been complaining about, and no amount of prompt tuning would have revealed it.

beats.broke: The model is stateless, so resending the whole history is the obvious fix — until it outgrows the window and truncation silently removes the instructions and the original goal.
beats.fix: Own the memory: write durable facts to storage as they happen, retrieve per turn what the current message needs, summarise from the record rather than from the last summary.
beats.cost: Forgetting is mandatory because the window is finite, so the only question is which forgetting you chose — and stale carried facts keep being recited until something expires them.

interview.q: Where does the memory in a conversational system actually live, and what breaks when you get it wrong?
interview.trap: Treating a growing transcript as memory. It degrades silently — truncation takes the oldest content, which is where the instructions were — and the decline gets blamed on the model.
